gist: Opens Chapter II by stating the simple theory of transmutation: what is transmuted is not species but their common subject, the mercurial first matter, which art must reduce and free, and which once freed is also the transmuting agent. Atwood then sets out to identify this mercury, turning to the ancient doctrine of the Ether or hidden fire and to the few moderns who held it without being able to prove it.

notes.point: Epigraph: all the wise seek is in Mercury.
The theory is simple: a pure matter in nature, perfected by art, converts to itself proportionally all imperfect bodies it touches.
Ground of transmutation: all natures share one radical substance and can be reduced to a common mercurial first matter, occult and undiscoverable by ordinary analysis.
Objection: species cannot change; gold infused into lead gives only a mixed middle nature, so transmutation is sophistical.
notes.voice: QUOTED: unnamed objectors (Atwood: rests on misunderstanding the alchemists)

notes.point: Alchemists accept this: not lead as lead (no more than dog into horse), but the subject-matter, the radical moisture of metals, is withdrawn by art from inferior Forms, freed by a superior ferment or attraction.

First work and foundation is Solution: reducing the body into water, i.e. mercury, argent vive. Subjects of species change only once reduced to first matter; then one form is expelled and another introduced, as glass from flints and ashes.
notes.voice: QUOTED: Friar Bacon; the author of the Rosarium (endorsed)

notes.point: Arnold, Avicenna, Aristotle concur; Ripley: metals transmute only reduced to their beginning, so liquable bodies may be mercurized.
Lully denies only a false version of the art.

The Universal Subject is both thing transmuted and, freed in its proper essentiality, thing transmuting. An adept: only the Light multiplies; perfected by art it exalts any body in its own kind; every body has passive principles for it, so nothing is borrowed from gold or silver.

This corrects the notion that alchemists extracted the Form from metals. Imputed follies (weighing elements, fixing metallic vapor by heat or sun and moon rays) were not theirs: they worked the one universal living occult nature by and through itself.

Lucerna Solis: one thing everywhere, no element yet able to become each, containing all nature; the Sages call it their salt, from their earth, not vulgar salt but salt of the world containing all Life; it makes the universal medicine.

Stone and medicine are one; only superfluities are removed. Geber: Sol reduced to mercury, nature embraces nature; the Stone is foetant spirit and living water, dry water. Aquinas: Mercury alone, root of gold and silver, dissolves, coagulates, colours, conceives and brings forth itself.
Nature is ordinarily known only in changes; alchemists claim to know her simple essence. Read their doctrine by this unity, not through metaphor. Atwood sets out to identify this mercury.
Ancient sages derived all from a pure hidden fire; the schools celebrated the all-pervading, perfective Ether governing nature; Virgil: spirit nourishes heaven, earth, stars.

Ethnic Anima Mundi differs from Hebrew doctrine only in words. Air holds a secret food of life moderns cannot isolate, so the One Element is derided. Homberg, Boerhaave, Boyle held a universal Ether ready to act on predisposed subjects; Berkeley called it pure invisible fire.

These moderns distinguished the fontal Spirit from its manifestation and from common fire (its mere excitation), but lacking proof and perhaps experience were disbelieved by a philosophy that supposes nothing not shown.

method.veiled: there abides in nature a certain pure matter, which, being discovered and brought by art to perfection, converts to itself proportionally all imperfect bodies that it touches
method.plain: The whole theory: there is one pure matter in nature; once found and perfected by art, it assimilates imperfect bodies to itself in proportion.
method.basis: I.2 ¶2 presents this as the basis of the theory.

method.veiled: the homogeneity of the radical substance of things
method.plain: All things, metals included, share one root substance; all can be reduced to this common basis, called the mercurial first matter.
method.basis: I.2 ¶3: 'may be reduced into their common basis or mercurial first matter'.

also.text: their common basis or mercurial first matter

method.veiled: the subject-matter of these metals, the radical moisture of which they are uniformly composed
method.plain: The art works on the common substance underlying species, not on the species (kinds) themselves.
method.basis: I.2 ¶4; restated I.2 ¶5 and I.2 ¶7.

also.text: Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime
the fundamental possibility and principle of transmutation being not of species, but of their Universal Subject or first matter

method.veiled: being set free by the force of a superior ferment or attraction
method.plain: The subject-matter is drawn out of the inferior forms by a stronger fermenting or attracting power.
method.basis: I.2 ¶4 only; this chunk does not say what the ferment is. I.2 ¶8 says the freed subject is itself 'the thing transmuting', which may be this ferment.

also.text: withdrawn by art and transported from inferior Forms

method.veiled: the first work is to reduce the body into water, that is, into mercury, and this is called Solution, which is the foundation of the whole art
method.plain: First step: Solution, reducing the body to its first matter, which is called 'water', 'mercury' or 'argent vive'.
method.basis: I.2 ¶5 glosses water as mercury and as argent vive.
method.voice: QUOTED: Friar Bacon; the author of the Rosarium (endorsed)

also.text: Solution and a reduction of the body into water, which is argent vive

method.veiled: one form being expelled, another may be introduced
method.plain: Once reduced to first matter, the subject is free to take a new form; the philosopher corrupts the old subject-matter and introduces a new Form, as glass is made from flints, stones and ashes.
method.voice: QUOTED: the author of the Rosarium (endorsed)

also.text: unless they are reduced first into their first matter, and made free to pass from one into another form
corrupt the Subject-matter of natures and to introduce a new Form

method.veiled: the Subject be freed by an artificial reduction
method.plain: The subject must be freed by art, by reducing it to its beginning; bodies so reduced become mercury ('mercurizate').
method.basis: I.2 ¶5-6: Ripley's verse sets 'reduced to their beginning materiable' as the condition for transmutation and concludes that such bodies 'may be mercurizate', i.e. turned to mercury (word not glossed in the text).

also.text: Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable
Mineral and metalline may be mercurizate

method.veiled: the thing transmuting also, when set free and segregated in its proper essentiality
method.plain: The same Universal Subject that is transmuted becomes the transmuting agent once it is freed and separated in its pure form.

method.veiled: It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied
method.plain: The active principle that multiplies and perfects is called 'the Light'; it comes from the first source of multiplication and generation.
method.basis: I.2 ¶8: the Light 'ascends and descends from the first fountain of multiplication and generation' and is 'discovered and perfected by art'. Its relation to the freed Universal Subject is unclear (see ambiguities).

also.text: This Light (discovered and perfected by art)

method.veiled: applied to any body, exalts and perfects it in its own kind
method.plain: The perfected Light improves whatever it is applied to within that thing's own kind: animals, vegetables, minerals. For minerals it raises them from worst to best condition.

also.text: translates them from the worst to the best condition

method.veiled: every body hath passive principles in itself for this Light to work upon
method.plain: No gold or silver is needed as an ingredient: every body already contains what the Light acts on. Atwood says this corrects the error that alchemists extracted the Form out of metals.

also.text: needs not to borrow any from gold or silver

method.veiled: weighing and proportioning the elements so exactly as to constitute them into lasting accord
method.plain: Literal readings (weighing elements, fixing metallic vapor with artificial heat or with sun and moon rays) are misunderstandings the adepts rejected; also the 'sulphur tingens' talk of impostors.
method.basis: I.2 ¶9 calls these 'literally imputed follies'; I.2 ¶8 rejects 'sulphur tingens' as fables.

also.text: consolidating the metalline vapor by heat artificially introduced, or by the rays of the sun and moon drawn to simultaneous cooperation
those imposters who tell you of a sulphur tingens

method.veiled: working, as it is said, the only universal living and occult nature by and through itself, scientifically
method.plain: The adepts' method works the one universal living nature by means of itself, not by outside agents; this let them follow nature and help her exceed her ordinary limits.
method.basis: I.2 ¶9; 'by and through itself' is consistent with I.2 ¶11, where Mercury works 'without foreign intervention' and dissolves, coagulates and conceives itself.

also.text: help her to exceed the ordinary limits of her law

method.veiled: The band of Sages only have known it, And they call it their salt.
method.plain: 'Their salt' is a name for the one universal thing found in everything, containing all nature and all Life. It is not common salt; it is extracted from 'their earth', which is not common earth.
method.basis: I.2 ¶9-10: the verse names the universal thing 'their salt' and contrasts it with 'the vulgar salt'. 'Their earth' is not explained in this chunk.

also.text: It is extracted from their earth
But rather the salt of the world, Which contains in itself all Life

method.veiled: It is not earth, nor fire, nor air, nor water
method.plain: The universal matter is none of the four elements, yet it can become any of them and take every opposite quality (white/red, hot/cold, moist/dry).

also.text: Nay it can become to be fire, air, water, and earth

method.veiled: Of it is made that medicine which will preserve you from all maladies
method.plain: The universal medicine is made from this salt of the world.

method.veiled: to which we add nothing nor take away anything, only in the preparation, removing superfluities
method.plain: The Stone is a single matter. The work adds nothing and removes nothing except superfluities during preparation.
method.basis: I.2 ¶11; also Aquinas's 'nothing different must be added'.
method.voice: QUOTED: the monk in his Rosary (endorsed)

also.text: The Stone is one
nothing different must be added

method.veiled: when Sol is reduced to his first original, i.e., the mercury, then nature embraceth nature
method.plain: When Sol is reduced to its first original, which is the mercury, 'nature embraceth nature'. This chunk does not say what Sol is or explain 'nature embraceth nature'.
method.basis: I.2 ¶11 glosses 'first original' as 'the mercury'.

method.veiled: our Stone is no other than a foetant spirit and living water, which we have named dry water
method.plain: The Stone is identified as a spirit and a 'living water', also called 'dry water', whose parts are cleansed and permanently united.
method.basis: I.2 ¶11. 'Foetant' is not explained.

also.text: by natural proportion cleansed and united with such union, that they can never more be absent each from other

method.veiled: It is Mercury alone which perfects in our work
method.plain: Only one matter, Mercury, is needed. It is the root of gold and silver, so it is not foreign to them, and it needs no partner ('sister') to serve as agent and patient.
method.basis: I.2 ¶11 gives 'it is their root' and 'without foreign intervention'. Reading it as agent and patient in one rests on I.2 ¶8 (the subject is 'the thing transmuting also'); the 'sister' sentence is defective (see ambiguities).

also.text: gold and silver are not unlike in kind to this our Mercury; for it is their root
if thou workest therefore with Mercury alone, without foreign intervention, thou obtainest thy desire

method.veiled: for it dissolves and coagulates itself ---whitens, rubifies, and makes itself to be both yellow and black
method.plain: The matter goes through its own changes (dissolution, coagulation, colour changes to white, red, yellow, black), then unites with, conceives and brings forth itself until it is perfected. This chunk gives no order for the colours.

also.text: The White and Red proceed from one root
it unites with itself, conceives itself, and brings itself forth, to the full perfecting of its intention

method.veiled: by no means be led aside by their metaphoric language into a common misconstruction of its meaning
method.plain: The texts' metaphors must be read in light of the one essential nature the alchemists claim to have found, not literally.

method.veiled: a certain pure and hidden fire
method.plain: Right after setting out to identify the mercury, Atwood presents the ancients' Ether, a pure hidden fire, from which all things come and which pervades all things.
method.basis: I.2 ¶12 places this right after 'let us seek therefore if we may be able at all to identify this mercury'. This chunk does not state the identity outright (see ambiguities).

also.text: the occult virtues of the Ether; its all-pervading essence and perfective power
which he likewise calls ether, and a pure invisible fire

method.veiled: this mighty Ether moreover is always at hand, ready to break forth into action on predisposed subjects
method.plain: The Ether is always present and acts (fermenting, producing, destroying) on subjects prepared to receive it.
method.voice: QUOTED: Homberg, Boerhaave, Boyle (reported with approval)

method.veiled: the fontal Spirit of nature, apart from its manifestation
method.plain: Nature's source-spirit is distinct from its visible effects. Ordinary fire is not this fire but only an excitation or effect of it.
method.basis: I.2 ¶15: 'they do not allow that to be fire indeed, but an excitation only or effect of the antecedent potency'.

also.text: an excitation only or effect of the antecedent potency

method.veiled: which in part it was perhaps, in their minds, without experience
method.plain: The moderns' Ether theory stayed speculative because they had no experience of it and no tangible proof. Atwood contrasts this with the alchemists, who claim 'another experience'.
method.basis: I.2 ¶15; contrast I.2 ¶12 'these alchemists profess to have enjoyed another experience'.

also.text: But then they could adduce no tangible proof of their doctrine.

ambiguities.quote: the thing transmuting also, when set free and segregated in its proper essentiality, the fermented Spirit assimilates the Light throughout
readings: The freed Universal Subject is the fermented Spirit, which assimilates (makes like itself) the Light throughout.
The freed Universal Subject, as fermented Spirit, is itself the Light that the adept's quote then calls the only multipliable thing.
ambiguities.basis: The sentence is textually defective (the phrase 'the thing transmutable in natures, as is above' is duplicated) and its syntax breaks. The adept's quote that follows makes the Light the multiplying agent, which suggests reading 2, but no explicit identity is stated.

ambiguities.quote: Some, mistaking, believe that the work cannot be perfected with mercury alone without his sister (i.e., as agent and patient) that thou addest nothing different from mercury
readings: The mistaken view needs a second substance (the 'sister') paired with mercury as agent and patient; the correct view is that mercury alone serves as both.
The parenthesis glosses the pair mercury-and-sister as agent and patient, without saying which is which.
ambiguities.basis: Words are evidently missing before 'that thou addest'. The context ('nothing different must be added'; it 'conceives itself, and brings itself forth') supports reading 1.

ambiguities.quote: let us seek therefore if we may be able at all to identify this mercury, and whether the same ancient material be yet on earth
readings: Atwood is preparing to identify the philosophers' mercury with the Ether, or pure hidden fire.
She is only surveying analogous ancient and modern doctrines without asserting an identity yet.
ambiguities.basis: The Ether discussion (I.2 ¶12-15) follows immediately, but no sentence in this chunk says mercury is the Ether.

ambiguities.quote: It is extracted from their earth
readings: 'Their earth' is a figurative source distinct from common earth.
It is some particular matter the Sages work on, left unnamed.
ambiguities.basis: I.2 ¶10 says only that 'the common earth is worth nothing here'.

ambiguities.quote: which in part it was perhaps, in their minds, without experience
readings: The moderns' Ether doctrine was partly mere speculation because they had no experience of it.
Atwood implies that the alchemists had such experience, which is the difference.
ambiguities.basis: I.2 ¶12: alchemists 'profess to have enjoyed another experience'. I.2 ¶15 does not state the contrast directly.

translations.original: Species non transmutantur, sed subjecta specierum optime et propriisime
translations.translation: Species are not transmuted, but the subjects of species are, most fittingly and properly.

translations.original: Species non transmutari sed individual specierum
translations.translation: That species are not transmuted, but the individuals of species.

translations.original: As the Philosopher who in the Book of Meteors did wryte, That the likeness of bodyes metallyne be not transmutable. But afterwards he added theis words of more delyte, Without they be reduced to their beginning materiable; Wherefore such bodies as in nature be liquable Mineral and metalline may be mercurizate, Conceive ye may theis science is not opinable, But very true by Raymond and others determinate
translations.translation: As the Philosopher wrote in the Book of Meteors, the likeness (kind) of metallic bodies is not transmutable. But afterwards he added these more pleasing words: unless they are reduced to their material beginning. Therefore mineral and metallic bodies that are naturally fusible may be turned into mercury. You may understand that this science is not mere opinion, but very true, as Raymond and others have determined.

translations.original: Elementiva habent vera conditiones et una species se non transmutet in aliam
translations.translation: species are absolute and cannot be changed one into another

translations.original: Elementiva habent vera conditiones et una species se non transmutet in aliam
translations.translation: Elemented things have true conditions, and one species does not transmute itself into another.

translations.original: Principio coelum, ac terras, composque liquentes, Lucentemque globum Lunae, Titaniaque astra, Spiritus intus alit; totamque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem, et magno se corpore miscet
translations.translation: In the first place, a spirit within nourishes the heaven and the lands and the watery plains, the shining globe of the Moon and the Titanian stars; and mind, poured through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body.

threads.note: 'as is above shown': points back to I.2 ¶3-7, which argue that the Universal Subject is the thing transmutable.

Atwood says the whole doctrine must be considered 'with reference to this presumed unity', and she sets out to identify the philosophers' mercury and whether 'the same ancient material be yet on earth'. Continued beyond this chunk.
Ends with 'how then should she recognize that recondite fire?': philosophy's failure to recognize the invisible fire, presumably taken up in the next chunk.
